title: Explain the role of DHCP and DNS

questions.question: Which statement is correct about reverse lookups?
choices: A reverse lookup is when the request needs to be reversed to another DNS server.
A reverse lookup is the resolution of an IP address to FQDN.
A reverse lookup is when the DNS queried can answer the request without asking another DNS server.
A reverse lookup is the resolution of an FQDN to an IP address.

correct.explanation: Reverse DNS resolves an IP address to an FQDN — forward DNS maps names to addresses.

incorrect.explanation: Forwarding to another DNS server is recursion/referral — reverse lookup specifically means IP-to-name resolution.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Defining reverse lookup as server referral
incorrect.whatItDoes: A reverse lookup is when the request needs to be reversed to another DNS server. names a DHCP DORA message step that may not be the phase described in the stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", A reverse lookup is the resolution of an IP address to FQDN. satisfies what this question tests — A reverse lookup is when the request needs to be reversed to another DNS server. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Answering without recursion describes an authoritative response — reverse lookup is about query direction (IP → name).
incorrect.whatItDoes: A reverse lookup is when the DNS queried can answer the request without asking another DNS server. names a DHCP DORA message step that may not be the phase described in the stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", A reverse lookup is the resolution of an IP address to FQDN. satisfies what this question tests — A reverse lookup is when the DNS queried can answer the request without asking another DNS server. does not.

incorrect.explanation: FQDN-to-IP is forward DNS (A/AAAA records) — reverse uses PTR in in-addr.arpa zones.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Swapping forward and reverse DNS definitions
incorrect.whatItDoes: A reverse lookup is the resolution of an FQDN to an IP address. shifts the answer to IP/Layer 3 addressing instead of Ethernet MAC learning.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", A reverse lookup is the resolution of an IP address to FQDN. satisfies what this question tests — A reverse lookup is the resolution of an FQDN to an IP address. does not.

answerReview.examTip: Reverse DNS = IP → FQDN (PTR); forward = name → IP.

questions.question: Which record type is used for an IPv4 address mapping to FQDN for DNS queries?

correct.explanation: PTR records map an IPv4 address to an FQDN (reverse DNS) — forward name-to-IP uses A records.

incorrect.explanation: A records map hostname to IPv4 address (forward DNS) — IP-to-FQDN reverse lookup uses PTR in in-addr.arpa zones.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using A record for reverse IP-to-name lookup
incorrect.whatItDoes: The A record points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for dns.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "dns", The PTR record satisfies what this question tests — The A record does not.

incorrect.explanation: CNAME is an alias pointing one name to another hostname — it does not perform IP-to-FQDN reverse resolution.
incorrect.whatItDoes: The CName record points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for dns.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "dns", The PTR record satisfies what this question tests — The CName record does not.

incorrect.explanation: AAAA records map hostname to IPv6 — reverse IPv4-to-FQDN uses PTR, not AAAA.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing AAAA with IPv4 reverse PTR
incorrect.whatItDoes: The AAAA record points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for dns.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "dns", The PTR record satisfies what this question tests — The AAAA record does not.

answerReview.examTip: IP → name = PTR (reverse); name → IP = A (forward).

questions.question: What gets appended to hostname queries for DNS resolution?

correct.explanation: IOS appends the configured DNS domain name to unqualified hostnames before querying — ip domain-name.

incorrect.explanation: A DNS zone is the authoritative dataset — the router appends the domain suffix, not the zone object.
incorrect.whatItDoes: The DNS zone points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for appended.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "appended", The DNS domain name satisfies what this question tests — The DNS zone does not.

incorrect.explanation: HTTP host headers are unrelated — DNS resolution appends the domain name.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: HTTP host header as DNS suffix
incorrect.whatItDoes: The host header points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for appended.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "appended", The DNS domain name satisfies what this question tests — The host header does not.

incorrect.explanation: PTR records map IP→name — hostname queries append the domain name for forward lookup.
incorrect.whatItDoes: The hostname PTR record points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for appended.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "appended", The DNS domain name satisfies what this question tests — The hostname PTR record does not.

answerReview.examTip: Unqualified name router1 + domain example.com → query router1.example.com.

questions.question: Which is the most secure method of name resolution for routers and switches?

correct.explanation: Static hostname entries (ip host) avoid DNS spoofing/dependency — most secure for device name resolution on routers.

incorrect.explanation: DNS relies on external servers — less secure than locally defined static mappings for critical peers.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: DNS as most secure device name resolution
incorrect.whatItDoes: DNS points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for resolution.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "resolution", Static hostname entries satisfies what this question tests — DNS does not.

incorrect.explanation: PTR records are reverse DNS — they do not replace secure static hostname tables on devices.
incorrect.whatItDoes: PTR records points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for resolution.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "resolution", Static hostname entries satisfies what this question tests — PTR records does not.

incorrect.explanation: LLMNR is a broadcast/multicast fallback — not the most secure enterprise method.
incorrect.whatItDoes: LLMNR points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for resolution.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "resolution", Static hostname entries satisfies what this question tests — LLMNR does not.

answerReview.examTip: Device peer names you must trust → ip host static table; lab DNS is fine for general lookup.

questions.question: Which type of DNS record holds the IPv4 IP address for a hostname?

correct.explanation: A records hold the IPv4 address for a hostname — the primary forward DNS mapping for IPv4 hosts.

incorrect.explanation: CNAME creates an alias to another DNS name — it does not directly store the IPv4 address.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using CNAME to store IPv4 address
incorrect.whatItDoes: The CName record points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for hostname.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "hostname", The A record satisfies what this question tests — The CName record does not.

incorrect.explanation: PTR records map IP to hostname (reverse DNS) — forward hostname-to-IPv4 uses A records.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Selecting PTR for forward IPv4 lookup
incorrect.whatItDoes: The PTR record points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for hostname.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "hostname", The A record satisfies what this question tests — The PTR record does not.

incorrect.explanation: AAAA records store IPv6 addresses — IPv4 hostname resolution uses A records.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Choosing AAAA for IPv4 hostname mapping
incorrect.whatItDoes: The AAAA record points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for hostname.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "hostname", The A record satisfies what this question tests — The AAAA record does not.

answerReview.examTip: Hostname → IPv4 = A record; IPv6 = AAAA; reverse = PTR.

questions.question: What limits the amount of time that a DNS entry is available in the DNS cache?

correct.explanation: TTL (Time To Live) on DNS records limits how long resolvers cache an entry before re-querying.

incorrect.explanation: An A record maps name→IPv4 — TTL controls cache duration, not the record type.
incorrect.whatItDoes: An A record points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for available.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "available", TTL satisfies what this question tests — An A record does not.

incorrect.explanation: SOA starts a zone and holds zone timers — per-record cache expiry is the record's TTL.
incorrect.whatItDoes: SOA points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for available.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "available", TTL satisfies what this question tests — SOA does not.

incorrect.explanation: There is no universal 5-minute default — each record's TTL field sets cache lifetime.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Default of 5 minutes points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for available.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "available", TTL satisfies what this question tests — Default of 5 minutes does not.

answerReview.examTip: DNS cache aging → check the record's TTL value (seconds until refresh).

questions.question: Which message is sent from the DHCP client to the DHCP server to confirm the offer of an IP address?

correct.explanation: After receiving an Offer, the client sends DHCPACK-bound DHCP Request, then ACK confirms the lease (DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledgment).

incorrect.explanation: Discover starts the process — confirmation of the offered address is the final ACK.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Discover names a DHCP DORA message step that may not be the phase described in the stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: DHCP message order (dns): Acknowledgment is the step this stem describes — Discover is another DORA phase.

incorrect.explanation: Offer is sent by the server — the client's confirm step is ACK after Request.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Offer names a DHCP DORA message step that may not be the phase described in the stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: DHCP message order (dns): Acknowledgment is the step this stem describes — Offer is another DORA phase.

incorrect.explanation: Request asks for the offered IP — the server replies with ACK to confirm the lease.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Request names a DHCP DORA message step that may not be the phase described in the stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: DHCP message order (dns): Acknowledgment is the step this stem describes — Request is another DORA phase.

answerReview.examTip: DORA order: Discover → Offer → Request → Ack — ACK is server confirmation to client.

questions.question: What form of communication does a DHCP client use to initially acquire an IP address?

correct.explanation: Initial DHCPDISCOVER is a Layer 3 broadcast (255.255.255.255) because the client has no IP yet.

incorrect.explanation: DHCP discover is not multicast — without an address the client must broadcast.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Layer 3 multicast gives a broadcast or multicast MAC pattern that may not be the all-ones form tested here.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Ethernet addressing (communication): Layer 3 broadcast is the broadcast/multicast form this stem expects — Layer 3 multicast uses the wrong MAC pattern.

incorrect.explanation: 802.1Q is VLAN tagging — DHCP discover uses UDP broadcast at Layer 3.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Layer 3 802.1Q expects VLAN tags on a link that should behave as access-only in this stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "communication", Layer 3 broadcast satisfies what this question tests — Layer 3 802.1Q does not.

incorrect.explanation: Unicast requires a known destination IP — pre-lease acquisition uses broadcast.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Layer 3 unicast points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for communication.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "communication", Layer 3 broadcast satisfies what this question tests — Layer 3 unicast does not.

answerReview.examTip: No IP yet → DHCP broadcast discover; relay (ip helper-address) forwards to server.

questions.question: At what point of the lease time will the client ask for a renewal of the IP address from the DHCP server?

correct.explanation: Clients begin renewal at 50% (T1) of lease time — unicast DHCPREQUEST to the leasing server.

incorrect.explanation: One-quarter is before the standard renewal point — T1 renewal starts at half the lease.
incorrect.whatItDoes: One-quarter of the lease points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for dns.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "dns", One-half of the lease satisfies what this question tests — One-quarter of the lease does not.

incorrect.explanation: Seven-eighths (T2) is rebinding if the original server is unreachable — first renewal is at 50%.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Seven-eighths of the lease points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for dns.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "dns", One-half of the lease satisfies what this question tests — Seven-eighths of the lease does not.

incorrect.explanation: Waiting until lease expires causes an outage — renewal at 50% prevents lapse.
incorrect.whatItDoes: End of the lease points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for dns.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "dns", One-half of the lease satisfies what this question tests — End of the lease does not.

answerReview.examTip: DHCP lease timers: T1 = 50% renew to server | T2 = 87.5% rebind | expiry = drop.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about the DHCP process?
choices: The DHCP server is responsible for maintaining the life cycle of an IP address.
DHCP uses multicasting between the client and server.
The DHCP client is responsible for maintaining the life cycle of an IP address.
The DHCP lease is negotiated between client and server.

correct.explanation: The DHCP client must renew or release before lease expiry — lifecycle maintenance (renew/rebind/release) is client-driven.

incorrect.explanation: The server tracks lease database and offers addresses, but the client initiates renewal at 50%/87.5% timers — lifecycle action is client-side.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Assigning all lifecycle responsibility to the server
incorrect.whatItDoes: The DHCP server is responsible for maintaining the life cycle of an IP address. shifts the answer to IP/Layer 3 addressing instead of Ethernet MAC learning.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", The DHCP client is responsible for maintaining the life cycle of an IP address. satisfies what this question tests — The DHCP server is responsible for maintaining the life cycle of an IP address. does not.

incorrect.explanation: DHCP discover/request use broadcast; offer/ack are often unicast — it is not general multicast between client and server.
incorrect.whatItDoes: DHCP uses multicasting between the client and server. gives a broadcast or multicast MAC pattern that may not be the all-ones form tested here.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", The DHCP client is responsible for maintaining the life cycle of an IP address. satisfies what this question tests — DHCP uses multicasting between the client and server. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Leases are offered by the server — "negotiated" overstates client/server haggling; the keyed distinction here is who maintains renewal lifecycle.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Focusing on negotiation wording instead of client renewal duty
incorrect.whatItDoes: The DHCP lease is negotiated between client and server. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", The DHCP client is responsible for maintaining the life cycle of an IP address. satisfies what this question tests — The DHCP lease is negotiated between client and server. does not.

answerReview.examTip: DHCP DORA — client sends Discover/Request; client renews before lease expires.

questions.question: Which transport protocol does DHCP use?

correct.explanation: DHCP uses UDP — client to server on 67, server to client on 68.

incorrect.explanation: ICMP is for diagnostics (ping) — DHCP discovery/offer uses UDP.
incorrect.whatItDoes: ICMP names a transport protocol or port behavior that may not match reliability or connection requirements.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Transport protocol (transport): UDP matches reliability, ports, or connection behavior — ICMP picks the wrong L4 protocol or port role.

incorrect.explanation: DHCP is connectionless UDP, not TCP — no three-way handshake for lease exchange.
incorrect.whatItDoes: TCP names a transport protocol or port behavior that may not match reliability or connection requirements.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: Transport protocol (transport): UDP matches reliability, ports, or connection behavior — TCP picks the wrong L4 protocol or port role.

incorrect.explanation: RARP is obsolete for IP assignment — modern networks use DHCP over UDP.
incorrect.whatItDoes: RARP points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for transport.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "transport", UDP satisfies what this question tests — RARP does not.

answerReview.examTip: DHCP = UDP/67 (server) + UDP/68 (client) | IPv6 DHCP uses UDP 546/547.

questions.question: What happens when a router or switch detects a duplicate IP address for a DHCP process?
choices: The IP address is still served to the client.
The IP address is removed from the DHCP pool.
The DHCP will serve the IP address in the future.

correct.explanation: On duplicate IP detection, IOS removes the address from the DHCP pool — prevents serving a conflicting lease.

incorrect.explanation: Serving a known duplicate would cause IP conflicts — IOS pulls the address from the pool.
incorrect.whatItDoes: The IP address is still served to the client. shifts the answer to IP/Layer 3 addressing instead of Ethernet MAC learning.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: This is a Layer 2 process (a router or switch detects a duplicate IP address for a DHCP process). The IP address is removed from the DHCP pool. uses Ethernet addresses — not IP headers.

incorrect.explanation: The DHCP service keeps running — only the conflicting address is excluded.
incorrect.whatItDoes: The DHCP server will halt. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for a router or switch detects a duplicate IP address for a DHCP process.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "a router or switch detects a duplicate IP address for a DHCP process", The IP address is removed from the DHCP pool. satisfies what this question tests — The DHCP server will halt. does not.

incorrect.explanation: The address is removed immediately, not deferred for future use.
incorrect.whatItDoes: The DHCP will serve the IP address in the future. shifts the answer to IP/Layer 3 addressing instead of Ethernet MAC learning.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: This is a Layer 2 process (a router or switch detects a duplicate IP address for a DHCP process). The IP address is removed from the DHCP pool. uses Ethernet addresses — not IP headers. Picking The DHCP will serve the IP address in the future. misses the exact behavior this stem tests.

answerReview.examTip: DHCP duplicate: ip dhcp conflict logging + address removed from pool — check with show ip dhcp conflict.
